Urea fertilizer is a critical agricultural input necessary for domestic crop production and the maintenance of the U.S. food supply chain. Current market conditions reflect significant supply disruptions and shortages of urea fertilizer within the United States due to international supply interruptions associated with the closure and disruption of traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, combined with insufficient available Jones Act-qualified vessel capacity capable of transporting this product.

Industry analyses have noted that a substantial portion of globally traded urea exports normally transit from producing regions dependent upon the Strait of Hormuz shipping corridor. The American Farm Bureau Federation and The Fertilizer Institute (TFI) have both reported that nearly one-half of global exportable urea supply is associated with this region and shipping route. Resulting disruptions have materially constrained fertilizer availability and increased the urgency of maintaining uninterrupted domestic supply movements.

Transportation by foreign-flag vessel pursuant to the March 17, 2026 Jones Act waiver is necessary because qualified Jones Act tonnage suitable for this movement is presently unavailable and committed to other domestic transportation activities. Reliable fertilizer supply is directly tied to domestic agricultural production and food security. Ensuring timely movement of this cargo therefore supports the national defense interests identified in the waiver by helping maintain continuity of the U.S. agricultural and food supply chain during a period of international supply disruption and limited domestic vessel availability.

Owner/Operator of Vessel: Clean Products Tankers Alliance (CPTA) / PRODUCTS TANKERS MANAGEMENT COMPANY INC
Explanation of National Defense Interest:
The vessel, Seaways Kolberg was identified as carrying off-specification jet fuel upon completion of load, which rendered the cargo unsuitable for delivery to its intended recipient. As a result, alternative disposition options were urgently evaluated.
At the time of discovery, the only readily available option was to discharge the cargo back into the original shore tank at Baytown Refinery. However, this action would have contaminated the remaining on-specification product within the tank, significantly reducing available supply to critical receivers in the region and compromising jet fuel inventory intended for service at the local airport.
In order to prevent disruption of fuel supply to critical consumers, preserve aviation fuel availability, and avoid contamination of otherwise usable inventory, the cargo was sold as a downgraded product to a receiver with sufficient available ullage and the capability to safely accept the off-specification material.
Given the circumstances, the inability to deliver the cargo as originally intended, and the substantial adverse impacts that would have resulted from returning the product to the originating shore tank, we respectfully request consideration of a Jones Act waiver. Granting this waiver would support the continued movement and disposition of the affected cargo in a manner that protects regional fuel supply, minimizes operational disruption, and serves the public interest.
